paraphrase:
The function has to decide whether a string is a well-formed JSON number: an optional minus, then an integer part that is either a single 0 or a nonzero digit followed by any digits, then optionally a point with one or more digits, then optionally an exponent letter, an optional sign and one or more digits. Anything that strays from this shape is invalid.

The submission first drops a single leading minus sign and returns False if nothing is left. It then finds the first exponent letter and separates the mantissa from the exponent text, and separates the mantissa at its first decimal point. A small nested helper judges the integer part: it must consist only of digits and must be either exactly the character 0 or not start with 0. A fraction, when a point is present, must be a non-empty run of digits. For the exponent, one optional plus or minus is removed and what remains must be a non-empty run of digits.

To test this beyond the three examples, I followed a few other strings. The string -0.25E+3 becomes a mantissa of 0.25 and an exponent of +3; the integer part 0 is allowed, 25 is all digits, and after the sign is dropped the exponent is the digit 3, so the result is True, matching the grammar. A lone minus sign leaves nothing to check and is rejected. The string 1.e5 has an empty fraction and is refused, which is correct because the grammar requires a digit after the point. In 1E5e3 the split happens at the lowercase letter, so the integer part becomes 1E5, which fails the all-digits test. Each check corresponds to one rule of the grammar rather than to any particular example.
